analysis.one_liner: Grants to help nonprofits and residents buy and preserve manufactured home communities with rent limits.
analysis.headline: The Manufactured Housing Community Preservation Act was introduced on January 7, 2020 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new grant program at the Department of Housing and Urban Development to help nonprofits, public housing agencies, tribes, and resident organizations buy manufactured home communities — the places where people own their home but rent the lot underneath it. Grantees would have to keep the land affordable for at least 20 years, limit annual lot rent increases, and maintain quality of life for residents. It authorized $100 million a year for five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities, most of whom own their home but rent the lot under it, often on low or fixed incomes. The bill gives resident groups and nonprofits grant money and a fair shot at buying their community when it comes up for sale, instead of losing out to investor buyers who raise lot rents afterward. Grantees in areas with many low-income families would get priority.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents renting their lots

how_it_helps.text: Creates a HUD grant program for acquiring and preserving manufactured housing communities, open to nonprofits including land trusts, public housing agencies, tribes, and resident-owned organizations.

Requires any community bought with grant funds to stay a manufactured housing community for at least 20 years, with limits on annual lot rent increases, management that benefits residents, and repayment of the grant if the deal is not honored.
Prioritizes grants for communities in areas with high concentrations of low-, very low-, and extremely low-income families, and allows funds to replace dilapidated homes.
Speeds up federal decisions to within 20 business days so applicants can act on real-world sale opportunities.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund up to $100 million a year for five years if Congress appropriates the money. Grantees would also have to raise matching funds equal to the federal grant from state, local, or private sources. Owners selling manufactured home communities would face new competition from resident and nonprofit buyers backed by federal money.

drawbacks.text: Each grantee must come up with matching funds equal to or exceeding the federal grant, a steep bar for small nonprofits or volunteer resident groups that the program is meant to help.

Grants are capped at the lesser of $1 million or $20,000 per lot, which in many markets is not enough to actually buy a community; the grant works only where a buyer can cover most of the purchase price.
The bill only authorizes spending; Congress would still have to pass a separate appropriations law each year to make the money available.
The rent limit allows annual increases up to the Consumer Price Index plus 7 percent, which permits substantial rent growth even on the protected lots.
Requiring HUD to approve or deny each application within 20 business days creates pressure for quick, thin vetting of applicants' capacity and finances.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is modest in scale relative to the problem: $100 million a year is small against a manufactured housing stock of many millions of homes, and the matching-fund and grant-size limits mean it would help scattered communities rather than reshape the market. But the design is targeted and accountable — the 20-year affordability strings, rent limits, and grant repayment requirement guard against the money just enriching buyers. The strongest objection is not that the program is wasteful but that it is undersized and hard to access for exactly the small, undercapitalized resident groups it aims to empower.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died at the end of the 116th Congress without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Representative Cynthia Axne introduced the Manufactured Housing Community Preservation Act of 2020 on January 7, 2020, together with Representative Ro Khanna.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and that is the only action the record shows; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.

The bill would have directed HUD to award grants to nonprofits, public housing agencies, tribes, and resident organizations to acquire and preserve manufactured housing communities, with a 20-year affordability requirement and limits on annual lot rent increases.
The program was authorized at $100 million per year for fiscal years 2021 through 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo. Owners and investors who buy manufactured home communities and raise lot rents face no new competition from resident or nonprofit buyers, and taxpayers were spared the $100 million annual cost. Residents of manufactured home communities gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Park investors and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Cynthia Axne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and reported the bill out of committee in over a year after referral, letting it die when the 116th Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is measurable; sponsorship came entirely from Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor joined.

industries.industry: Manufactured housing community owners and investors
industries.note: The bill would put federal grant money behind nonprofit, resident, and public buyers competing for communities when they come up for sale, and would cap lot rent increases at CPI plus 7 percent on purchased communities. Investors who profit from buying parks and raising lot rents on captive homeowners — people who own their home but cannot move it cheaply — would face a cheaper rival buyer and rent limits.

industries.industry: Nonprofit housing and community development organizations
industries.note: The bill creates a dedicated funding stream that these groups could use to acquire and preserve communities, which they could otherwise rarely outbid investors to do. The matching-fund requirement would favor the more capitalized among them.

Grant funds could be used to demolish, remove, and replace dilapidated homes in preserved communities, creating replacement orders for home manufacturers. Residents get better housing; builders get sales.
